Proofs about Composite Functions

Glue two functions together and inspect the composite with tables and arrows. See what the composite's properties force onto each part.

If the composite is injective, the first function is injective too. If the composite is surjective, the second function is surjective. The converses fail, and the diagrams show why. Undoing a composite also reverses the order.

For example, pack a 📦 box, close the lid, then tie it with string. To open it, the string comes off first. The last step done is the first step undone. That is why inverses of composites reverse the order.

f(a1)=f(a2)  ⟹  g(f(a1))=g(f(a2))f(a_1) = f(a_2) \implies g(f(a_1)) = g(f(a_2))f(a1​)=f(a2​)⟹g(f(a1​))=g(f(a2​))
(g∘f)−1=f−1∘g−1(g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}(g∘f)−1=f−1∘g−1

Prove completely that if g∘fg \circ fg∘f is surjective then ggg is surjective.

Then use the scene's surjective-chain tables (f=[0,1]f = [0,1]f=[0,1], g=[0,1,0]g = [0,1,0]g=[0,1,0], B=[0,1,2]B = [0,1,2]B=[0,1,2]) to check why fff fails to be surjective (it misses 222) while the composition g∘f=[0,1]g \circ f = [0,1]g∘f=[0,1] still covers all of CCC.

Show proof

  1. Take any c∈Cc \in Cc∈C.

    Since g∘fg \circ fg∘f is surjective, there is a∈Aa \in Aa∈A with g(f(a))=cg(f(a)) = cg(f(a))=c.

    Setting b=f(a)∈Bb = f(a) \in Bb=f(a)∈B gives g(b)=g(f(a))=cg(b) = g(f(a)) = cg(b)=g(f(a))=c — so ccc has a ggg-preimage, and ggg is surjective.

    In the picture: if the composite arrows hit every point of CCC, the later arrows must too.

  2. The first map fff need not be surjective: in this example f=[0,1]f = [0,1]f=[0,1] misses the element 222 of BBB and is not surjective, yet g=[0,1,0]g = [0,1,0]g=[0,1,0] hits both elements of CCC via g(0)=0g(0) = 0g(0)=0, g(1)=1g(1) = 1g(1)=1, so the composition g∘f=[0,1]g \circ f = [0,1]g∘f=[0,1] is surjective.
